title: Corporate sustainability

definition.text: A business approach that aims to create long-term value for stakeholders by building ethical, social, environmental, cultural and economic concerns into company strategy.

facts.text: It is often confused with corporate social responsibility, but scholars say the key difference is time: sustainability asks firms to make trade-offs across time to protect future generations.
The idea grew out of sustainable development, as defined by the Brundtland Commission, and John Elkington's 1997 'triple bottom line'.
In the research literature it is usually treated as a three-part idea combining social, environmental and economic factors.
Its most widely accepted test is whether a firm uses natural capital efficiently, including keeping vital ecosystem services such as climate regulation and water purification.
Firms often state their commitment through Corporate Sustainability Standards, policies meant to meet or go beyond minimum legal requirements.
Whether it can be measured is disputed, because there is no generally accepted set of indicators separating sustainable from unsustainable operation.
Short-term thinking is described as the main enemy of corporate sustainability.

contested_note: Sources say it remains contested whether corporate sustainability can be measured at all.

definition.text: Eco-efficiency compares the economic value a firm adds with its total ecological impact; socio-efficiency compares that value with the firm's social impact.

facts.text: Most corporate effects on the environment are assumed to be negative, while social effects can be positive, such as job creation, or negative, such as work accidents.
Both measures mainly aim at economic sustainability, treating natural and social capital as tools for win-win gains.
Some authors argue sustainable development instead needs eco-effectiveness, socio-effectiveness, sufficiency and eco-equity.

title: Creating shared value

definition.text: A business strategy in which a company seeks profit by solving social problems linked to its own operations, improving its competitiveness and the conditions of its communities at once.

facts.text: Michael Porter and Mark Kramer introduced the idea in a 2006 Harvard Business Review article and expanded it in a January 2011 follow-up.
Companies can create shared value in three ways: reconceiving products and markets, redefining productivity in the value chain, and enabling local cluster development.
Kramer says the main difference from corporate social responsibility is that CSR is about responsibility, while shared value is about creating value.
Accounting for ecological costs is hard: up to 90% of the ecological footprint in food processing comes from land management outside corporations' control.
Counting ecosystem services at the farm level lets shared value include positive environmental externalities in the economic system.
Reviewers found little rigorous analysis of its impact; most evidence comes from standalone case studies of mixed quality.
The Economist called the concept 'undercooked', and a common criticism is that it plays down the trade-offs businesses must make.
Critics have noted its 'striking resemblance' to Jed Emerson's earlier idea of blended value.

related: Bottom of the pyramid and inclusive business
contested_note: Porter presents shared value as a win-win, while critics such as The Economist call it undercooked and say it ignores trade-offs.

title: Bottom of the pyramid and inclusive business

definition.text: Inclusive business models create value by selling products and services to the poor or buying from them, bringing poor people directly into companies' value chains.

facts.text: Shared value work has focused on the 'bottom of the pyramid' because this group has greater social needs and offers new markets.
Prahalad and Hart's paper 'The Fortune at the Bottom of the Pyramid' argued that serving poor consumers offers both commercial and social opportunities.
A classic example is Hindustan Unilever selling hygiene products in smaller package sizes suited to poor customers.
In an IFC survey, around 90% of 167 applicants named access to finance as a main obstacle to inclusive business models.

title: EU taxonomy for sustainable activities

definition.text: A European Union classification system that defines which economic activities count as environmentally sustainable, created under the European Green Deal.

facts.text: Its aim is to prevent greenwashing and help investors make informed sustainable investment decisions.
It covers six environmental objectives: climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, circular economy, pollution prevention, water and marine resources, and biodiversity and ecosystems.
The Taxonomy came into force in July 2020 as part of the European Green Deal, which aims for a carbon neutral economy by 2050.
A Technical Expert Group set up in 2018 developed the technical screening criteria used to judge whether an activity is sustainable.
The Environmental Delegated Act, published on 21 November 2023, set criteria for the remaining objectives, including protection and restoration of biodiversity and ecosystems.
Banks must disclose a 'green asset ratio'; early estimates put the EU banks' average at 2.23%.
An EU green bond standard under development would require issuers to fund activities aligned with the taxonomy.

related: Natural gas and nuclear in the EU taxonomy
notes: EU-wide regulation (Regulation 2020/852); kept as a multi-country framework seeded in this chapter.

title: Do no significant harm

definition.text: The rule that an activity counts as sustainable under the EU taxonomy only if it contributes substantially to one environmental objective without seriously harming any of the other five.

facts.text: An activity must meet four requirements: a substantial contribution to one objective, no significant harm to the others, minimum social safeguards, and the technical screening criteria.
The Technical Expert Group held back from including nuclear energy because it could not settle whether nuclear met this principle.

distinct_from: Natural gas and nuclear in the EU taxonomy

title: Natural gas and nuclear in the EU taxonomy
article: EU taxonomy for sustainable activities#Debate over natural gas and nuclear energy

definition.text: The dispute over whether fossil gas and nuclear power should be labelled as environmentally sustainable investments under the EU taxonomy.

facts.text: The Complementary Climate Delegated Act, the most controversial one, listed certain gas and nuclear activities as transitional activities that help mitigate climate change.
Expert advice split: the Technical Expert Group did not recommend including nuclear, while the Joint Research Centre found its impact would stay below harmful levels.
Some countries see gas as a bridge from coal to renewables, while the Netherlands, Austria, Sweden and Denmark opposed including it.
On 6 July 2022 a resolution to reject the act failed in the European Parliament: 278 MEPs backed it when 353 votes were needed.

contested_note: Member states, expert bodies and industry groups disagree on whether gas and nuclear power are sustainable.
